titulo: What they laugh at, and the joke you get to make
subtitulo: Mexican humour is fast, filthy and affectionate all at once — you can enjoy every bit of it without attempting the two moves that only land from an insider
cena: The whole table just detonated over a sentence about a spoon, everyone is looking at you, and you have about two seconds to decide what your face is doing.
frasePiso: You do not have to land the joke. Laughing at the right moment and asking what it meant is already being good company.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: The albur is a characteristic Mexican form of humour built on rapid sexual double meaning — an ordinary sentence is constructed so a second, obscene reading is available, and the exchange works as a competitive volley between speakers.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de fontes culturais (Mexperience — «So Do Mexicans Have a Sense of Humor?»; Matador Network — «9 Things You Need to Know to Understand Mexican Humor»)

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Mexican humour is widely self-deprecating and freely jokes about death and hardship, but three targets are commonly described as off-limits, especially from an outsider: national symbols, the Virgin of Guadalupe, and anyone's mother.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de fontes culturais (Matador Network; Mexperience)

steps.pt: Today is about laughing in the right places. Two of the moves are receptive only — you enjoy them, you don't perform them.
Six people at a table. Someone says something ordinary about a spoon and the table detonates. You missed it entirely.

steps.es: ¿Y tú qué, no le entras a la cuchara?
steps.pt: 👂 Not for you to decode. The second meaning is the joke, and it went past — that's expected.
steps.tts: ¿Y tú qué, no le entras a la cuchara?

steps.pt: That's an albur: an ordinary sentence built so an obscene reading sits inside it. People answer albur with albur.
You won't win that volley, and nobody expects you to. The honest move is to say you missed it and ask.

steps.promptPt: The table is laughing and you have no idea why. Say so, lightly. Speak now.
steps.pt: I didn't get it — explain it to me?

steps.es: Ay, no seas malpensado. Es albur.
steps.pt: Don't overthink it — it's an albur.
steps.tts: Ay, no seas malpensado. Es albur.

steps.pt: Asking made you part of it. Now the other half: what they joke about that surprises visitors.

steps.es: Nos vemos el dos de noviembre, si es que llego.
steps.pt: 👂 A joke about dying, said cheerfully. Death is ordinary comic material here, not a taboo.
steps.tts: Nos vemos el dos de noviembre, si es que llego.

steps.pt: Death and hardship are fair game, and so are they. Three things are not: national symbols, the Virgin of Guadalupe, and mothers.
Those land badly from a foreigner even when a local just said worse. That asymmetry is what insider licence means.

steps.promptPt: Someone made a sharp joke about their own city. Appreciate it without adding your own. Speak now.
steps.pt: That was really good.
And the joke that does land from you: yourself. Your accent, your confusion, your first taco. Self-deprecation travels.

steps.promptPt: Make the joke about your own Spanish, not about them. Speak now.
steps.es: Mi español todavía no aguanta el albur.
steps.pinyin: mee ehs-pah-NYOL toh-dah-BEE-ah noh ah-GWAHN-tah el ahl-BOOR
steps.pt: My Spanish can't handle albur yet.
steps.tts: Mi español todavía no aguanta el albur.

steps.pt: You're learning, huh.

steps.promptPt: They teased you back and it was friendly. Take it well, out loud. Speak now.
steps.pt: Fair enough, honestly.

steps.promptPt: You want to be able to use the word later. Ask what it means. Speak now.
steps.pt: What does that word mean?

steps.promptPt: A joke landed and you followed it. Say so. Speak now.
steps.pt: That one I did get.

steps.es: No le entendí, ¿me explicas? Estuvo buenísimo eso. Mi español todavía no aguanta el albur.
steps.pinyin: noh leh en-ten-DEE, meh eks-PLEE-kahs. ehs-TOO-boh bweh-NEE-see-moh EH-soh. mee ehs-pah-NYOL toh-dah-BEE-ah noh ah-GWAHN-tah el ahl-BOOR
steps.pt: Shadow the three safe moves: ask, appreciate, joke about yourself.
steps.tts: No le entendí, ¿me explicas? Estuvo buenísimo eso. Mi español todavía no aguanta el albur.

steps.pt: A02 complete. Albur and mother jokes stay receptive. Asking, appreciating and laughing at yourself are yours.

aprofundar.titulo: Insider licence is a real thing, and it isn't unfair

secoes.titulo: The albur is a sport, not a slur
secoes.corpo: It is competitive wordplay: an innocuous sentence engineered so an obscene reading is available, answered in kind. Speed is the whole point, which is exactly why a second-language speaker cannot join in — and why nobody expects you to.

secoes.titulo: Dark humour is warmth, not cynicism
secoes.corpo: Jokes about death, poverty and disaster are ordinary here, and they are a way of handling those things rather than dismissing them. Reacting with visible discomfort reads as pity, which lands worse than the joke ever would.

secoes.titulo: Three things a visitor should not joke about
secoes.corpo: National symbols, the Virgin of Guadalupe, and anybody's mother. A local may joke about all three in front of you; that is licence you do not have, and reaching for it is the fastest way to cool a warm table.
Yourself. Your accent, your first attempt at ordering, your face when the salsa arrived. Self-deprecation is the one comic register that reads the same in every language and costs nothing.

permissao: You are allowed to not get it, and to say so. Asking what a joke meant is not killing the joke — at a Mexican table it usually extends it, because now somebody gets to explain it badly and that's funny too.
espelho: Every language has a register only insiders can use — the joke your own friends make about your hometown that a visitor absolutely cannot. Mexican humour isn't unusually gated; you're just on the visiting side of the gate this time, which is a position you've granted other people your whole life.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Someone at the table makes a cheerful joke about death, or about being broke, and you find yourself unsure whether to laugh.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That was dark — laughing would be callous, so I should look sympathetic.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Dark humour is a normal and affectionate register in Mexican conversation, widely described as a way of handling hardship rather than denying it. The sympathetic face reads as pity, and pity is the one reaction the joke was built to avoid.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Laugh with it. If you want to say something, appreciate the joke rather than commenting on the subject of it.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stay inside the conversation instead of accidentally turning it solemn, which is what a visitor's concerned face does to a table that was having a good time.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when someone is plainly telling you about a real, current loss — the comic register and an actual confidence sound different, and the tell is that nobody else is laughing.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A local makes a savage joke about their own country, so you offer one of your own in the same spirit.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They opened that door, so it's clearly fine ground — joining in shows I'm comfortable with them.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Self-criticism from inside a group and the same criticism from a visitor are different speech acts, and only the first reads as affection. The asymmetry is sharper here because the self-deprecating joke is so constant that it can look like an open invitation.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Appreciate the joke out loud instead of matching it, and keep your own material aimed at yourself.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the warmth of the exchange without the one move that quietly costs you the table.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a rule against ever disagreeing or discussing anything serious — it is specifically about comic criticism of the country, which is theirs to make.
